planting.note: Tuck small divisions into cool, mossy, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring, keeping the shallow roots undisturbed and consistently moist until established.

directions: Naked miterwort is a diminutive boreal forest native found carpeting mossy, rotting logs and cool conifer duff across the northern tier of North America, forming loose colonies of small, rounded, evergreen leaves on creeping stolons. In late spring it sends up leafless, wiry flower stalks bearing tiny, intricately fringed, greenish-yellow flowers that are easy to overlook but rewarding under a hand lens. It thrives only in reliably cool, moist, acidic conditions with high humus content and struggles in warm-summer gardens south of its native range, making it best suited to shaded rock gardens, moss gardens, and stumperies in cool climates. Divide and replant small sections in spring rather than attempting to grow from seed, which is slow and erratic.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded streambank or seep, where the plant will self-sow into congenial damp crevices.

directions: Coast boykinia is a Pacific coastal native found along redwood-shaded streambanks, seeps, and damp rock outcrops from California to British Columbia, forming clumps of rounded, shallowly lobed, maple-like leaves topped by loose, airy panicles of small white, star-shaped flowers in late spring and early summer. It requires constant moisture and cool root conditions to perform well and will scorch or go dormant early if soil dries out, making it ideal for the wet, shaded margins of a woodland stream, pond, or rain garden. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome and self-sow into nearby damp crevices; combine with sword fern, redwood sorrel, and wild ginger for an authentic Pacific Northwest streamside planting. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; established clumps spread gently to form a tidy colony.

directions: Fortune's chloranthus is a Chinese woodland perennial closely related to the smaller, more commonly grown Chloranthus japonicus, distinguished by taller stems, glossier whorled leaves, and showier, more elongated brush-like spikes of tiny, fragrant white flowers composed almost entirely of stamens rather than true petals. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a neat, weed-suppressing colony beneath deciduous trees and pairs well with hellebores, hostas, and ferns in a refined shaded border. Give it evenly moist, humus-rich soil and protection from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the foliage in warmer parts of its range. Clumps are rarely bothered by deer or serious pests and can be divided in early spring every few years to expand the planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from drying wind.

directions: Japanese cardiandra is an unusual woodland relative of hydrangea from the cool, moist mountain forests of Japan, forming an herbaceous to semi-woody clump of broad, alternately arranged, coarsely toothed leaves topped in late summer by domed clusters of small, pale pink to lavender, hydrangea-like flowers. In colder gardens the topgrowth dies back to a woody crown each winter and resprouts in spring, behaving more like a herbaceous perennial than a true shrub. It demands the same cool, constantly moist, humus-rich conditions as astilbe or Deinanthe and resents both drought and waterlogging, rewarding attentive siting with a long season of interest from bold foliage through late-summer bloom. Site it in a sheltered woodland border alongside hostas, ferns, and Japanese forest grass where its unusual late bloom extends seasonal color after most shade perennials have finished.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade sheltered from wind; this white-flowered selection needs the same exacting cool woodland conditions as the species.

directions: 'Album' is a prized white-flowered selection of the monotypic Japanese woodland poppy, producing the same large, deeply palmate, maple-like leaves as the species but with pure white, single, poppy-like flowers 2-3 inches across instead of the typical mauve-lavender, brightened further by prominent golden stamens. Like the species it is slow to establish, resents root disturbance, and demands consistently cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade sheltered from wind and summer heat. The clean white bloom shows especially well against dark-leaved companions such as hellebores or Asian ferns in a shaded collector's border. Best suited to the Pacific Northwest, upper Midwest, and New England, where cool summers allow established plants to become long-lived, pest-free garden fixtures.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; 'Crimson Fans' colors best with some morning sun and consistent moisture.

directions: 'Crimson Fans' is a widely admired selection of mukdenia grown chiefly for its deeply lobed, fan-shaped leaves, which emerge fresh green in spring and develop striking crimson-red margins and tips as temperatures cool in autumn, eventually flushing almost entirely burgundy-red in a sharp frost. Airy, astilbe-like sprays of small white flowers appear on wiry stems just above the foliage in early spring before the leaves fully expand. More drought-tolerant than most shade perennials once established, it nonetheless performs best with reliable moisture and some protection from the hottest afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaf edges. Use it as a textural foliage accent at the front of a shaded border or alongside hostas and ferns, where its fan-shaped leaves and seasonal color shift provide interest from spring bloom through fall.
